APPENDIX B
List of mental disorders
This appendix consists of the list of mental disorders that were used as an inclusion criterion during screening. Any disorder found in the screening that was not on this list was excluded. 
LIST OF MENTAL DISORDERS for ADULTS
Neurodevelopmental Disorders
Intellectual Disabilities (Intellectual Disability (Intellectual Developmental Disorder), Global Developmental Delay)
Autism Spectrum Disorder (Autism Spectrum Disorder)
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder)
Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
(Schizotypal (Personality) Disorder, "Delusional Disorder", Brief Psychotic Disorder, Schizophrenia, Schizoaffective Disorder)
Bipolar and Related Disorders (Bipolar I Disorder, Bipolar II Disorder, Cyclothymic Disorder)
Depressive Disorders (Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder, Single and Recurrent Episodes, Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia))
Anxiety Disorders (Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia), Panic Disorder, Panic Attack (Specifier), Agoraphobia, Generalized Anxiety Disorder)
Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Body Dysmorphic Disorder, Hoarding Disorder, Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder), Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder)
Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders  (Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, Acute Stress Disorder)
Dissociative Disorders (Dissociative Identity Disorder)
Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders (Somatic Symptom Disorder, Illness Anxiety Disorder, Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder))
Feeding and Eating Disorders (Anorexia Nervosa, Bulimia Nervosa, Binge-Eating Disorder)
Elimination Disorders
Sleep-Wake Disorders (Insomnia Disorder, RLS)
Gender Dysphoria (Antisocial Personality Disorder)
Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
Personality Disorders (General Personality Disorder)

Cluster A Personality Disorders (Paranoid Personality Disorder, Schizoid Personality Disorder, Schizotypal Personality Disorder)
Cluster B Personality Disorders (Antisocial Personality Disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, Histrionic Personality Disorder, Narcissistic Personality Disorder)
Cluster C Personality Disorders (Avoidant Personality Disorder, Dependent Personality Disorder, Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder)
19 Paraphilic Disorders (Voyeuristic Disorder, Exhibitionistic Disorder, Frotteuristic Disorder, Sexual Masochism Disorder, Sexual Sadism Disorder, Pedophilic Disorder, Fetishistic Disorder, Transvestic Disorder)

LIST OF MENTAL DISORDERS for CHILDREN and ADOLESCENTS
Neurodevelopmental disorders
Intellectual disabilities (intellectual developmental disorder, global developmental delay)
Autism spectrum disorder (with an emphasis on Asperger´s disorder)
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) or Hyperkinetic Syndrome or Hyperkinetic Disorder
Communication Disorders (with emphasis in Language Disorder, Speech Sound Disorder, Childhood-Onset Fluency Disorder (Stuttering), Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder)
Specific learning disorders (with an emphasis in dyslexia)
Motor skills disorder (with an emphasis in Developmental coordination disorder)
Tic disorders (with an emphasis in Tourette´s disorder)
Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders (Schizophrenia, psychosis, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, schizoaffective)
Bipolar and related disorders (bipolar, cyclothymic disorder)
Depressive disorders (this and the previous are part of mood disorders, with emphasis in Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder)
Anxiety disorders (with emphasis in Separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, Phobia, Social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia)
Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders [obsessive-compulsive, Body Dysmorphic Disorder, Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder), Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder]
Trauma- and stressor-related disorders (with emphasis in Reactive Attachment Disorder; Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder)
Dissociative disorders (dissociative identity disorder)
Eating disorders (with an emphasis in anorexia, bulimia, binge eating, pica, Rumination Disorder, Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder)
Elimination disorders (with an emphasis in Enuresis and Encopresis)
Sleep-Wake disorders [with an emphasis in insomnia, parasomnias (with emphasis in sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, sleep terrors)
Gender dysphoria
Impulse-control disorders (with an emphasis in Oppositional defiant disorder, Intermittent Explosive Disorder and Conduct disorder)
Substance-related and addictive disorder

Appendix J 
Forest Plot for the outcome variable SOL actigraphy for children and adolescents in the Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder group & Comorbid Insomnia

Figure J1: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder group & Comorbid Insomnia













Appendix K
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed in children and adolescents with Autistic Spectrum Disorder
SOL 
For SOL diary there were k = 2 and N = 28, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -51.04, 95% CI [-59.57, -42.5], z = -11.72, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 1) = 0.001, p = 0.97, τ = 0, I2 = 0% which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. For SOL actigraphy there were k = 2 and N = 21, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -13.41, 95% CI [-19.9, -6.92], z = -4.05, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 1) = 0.68, p = 0.41, τ = 0, I2 = 0% which meant that this analysis did produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, both measurements of SOL appear to reduce after a treatment of melatonin in children and adolescents with ASD which would suggest that melatonin is more effective than placebo here. 


Figure K1: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD group

Figure K2: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL actigraphy scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD group



TST
TST diary data were analysed in the ASD group. For TST diary there were k = 2 and N = 28, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = 63.33, 95% CI [7.53, 78.58], z = 8.48, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 1) = 0.55, p = 0.46, τ = 0, I2 = 0%  which means that the total variability among effect sizes may be caused by “true” heterogeneity between studies and not by sampling error. Overall, TST diary appears to reduce after a treatment of melatonin in children and adolescents with ASD which would suggest that melatonin is more effective than placebo here. 


Figure K3: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD group

NA
NA analysis consisted of k = 3 and N = 40, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo SMD = -0.63, 95% CI [-1.65, 0.38], z = -1.22, p = 0.22. Therefore, this analysis indicates that the number of NAs may not reduce in children and adolescents with ASD after a period of melatonin treatment.


Figure K4: A forest plot to show the standardized means difference of NA scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD group

Appendix L
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed for children and adolescents in the Autistic Spectrum Disorder with Insomnia group 
SOL 
For SOL diary there were k = 3 and N = 128, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -44.56, 95% CI [-59.5, -29.61], z = -5.84, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 2) = 3.61, p = 0.16, τ = 9.22 I2 = 47.91% which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. For SOL actigraphy there were k = 3 and N = 87, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -23.3, 95% CI [-23.19, -39.58], z = -7.02, p = 0.01. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 2) = 8.21, p = 0.02, τ = 11.61, I2 = 72.45% which meant that this analysis did not produce an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, both measurements of SOL appear to reduce after treatment of melatonin in children and adolescents with ASD and ASD with insomnia which would suggest that melatonin is more effective than placebo here. However, the actigraphy results should be interpreted with caution as there is a lot of uncounted variability.












Figure L1: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD & ASD Comorbid Insomnia group

Figure L2: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL actigraphy scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD & ASD Comorbid Insomnia group





TST
Both TST diary and TST actigraphy data were analysed in the ASD & ASD Insomnia group. For TST diary there were k = 3 and N = 128, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = 58.9, 95% CI [44.13, 73.68], z = 7.8, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 2) = 1.65, p = 0.44, τ = 4.72, I2 = 51.44%  which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. For TST actigraphy there were k = 2 and N = 78, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = 51.5, 95% CI [11.91, 91.1], z = 2.55, p = 0.01. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 1) = 2.1, p = 0.15, τ = 22.25, I2 = 51.44%  which meant that this analysis did produce an output which can account for the variability of effect sizes. Overall, both measurements of TST appear to increase after a treatment of melatonin in children and adolescents with ASD and ASD with insomnia.





Figure L3: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD & ASD Comorbid Insomnia group








Figure L4: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST actigraphy scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD & ASD Comorbid Insomnia group













NA
NA analysis consisted of k = 4 and N = 106, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo SMD = -1.22, 95% CI [-2.56, 0.11], z = -1.8, p = 0.07. Therefore, this analysis indicates that the number of NAs may not reduce in children and adolescents with ASD and ASD with insomnia after a period of melatonin treatment.

Figure L5: A forest plot to show the standardized mean difference of NA scores for melatonin against placebo in the ASD & ASD Comorbid Insomnia group











Appendix M
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed for children and adolescents in the Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder group
SOL
For SOL diary there were k = 2 and N = 70, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -26.09, 95% CI [-43.61, -8.57], z = -2.92, p =0.004. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 1) = 1.72, p = 0.19, τ = 8.56, I2 = 41.87%  which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. For SOL actigraphy there were k = 3 and N = 87, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo MD = -13.75, 95% CI [-34.58, -7.08], z = -1.29, p = 0.2. Overall, SOL diary appears to reduce after a treatment of melatonin whilst SOL actigraphy does not reduce in children and adolescents with DSPD. 



Figure M1: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the DSPD group

Figure M2: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL actigraphy scores for melatonin against placebo in the DSPD group

TST
Both TST diary and TST actigraphy data were analysed in the DSPD group. For TST diary, there were k = 2 and N = 70, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo MD = 31.7, 95% CI [3.29, 60.12], z = 2.19, p = 0.29. Similarly, for TST actigraphy there were k = 2 and N = 70, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo MD = 20.58, 95% CI [-6.79, 47.95], z = 1.47, p = 0.14. Overall, this means that both outcome variables of TST appear not to differ after a treatment of melatonin in comparison to placebo, for children and adolescents with DSPD.

Figure M3: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the DSPD group

Figure M4: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST actigraphy scores for melatonin against placebo in the DSPD group














Appendix N
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed for children and adolescents in the Insomnia group
SOL
For SOL diary there were k = 4 and N = 221, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -22.9, 95% CI [-34.63, -11.16], z = -3.82, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 3) = 6.37, p = 0.1, τ = 8.69, I2 = 53.69%  which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, this result indicates that melatonin may reduce SOL diary scores by on average 22.9 minutes in children and adolescents with Insomnia in comparison to using placebo supplements.

Figure N1: A forest plot to show the mean difference of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the Insomnia group




TST
TST diary was analysed in the insomnia group, there were k = 4 and N = 168 and the results indicated a significant difference in favour melatonin over placebo MD = 31.54, 95% CI [22.45, 40.62], z = 6.8, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 3) = 5.19, p = 0.16, τ = 5.43, I2 = 31.54%  which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, this result indicates that melatonin may increase TST diary scores by on average 31.54 minutes in children and adolescents with Insomnia in comparison to using placebo.

Figure N2: A forest plot to show the mean difference of TST diary scores for melatonin against placebo in the Insomnia group








DLMO
Finally, DLMO was analysed in the insomnia group, there were k = 4 and N = 226, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo MD = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.81, 0.15], z = -1.32, p = 0.19. This meant that DLMO scores did not differ between melatonin and placebo after a period of treatment for children and adolescents with insomnia.

Figure N3: A forest plot to show the mean difference of DLMO scores for melatonin against placebo in the Insomnia group










Appendix O
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed for children and adolescents in the Neurodevelopmental Disorders with Comorbid Insomnia group
SOL

Appendix AB
A detailed description and forest Plots for all the outcome variables analysed in the sensitivity analyses for adult the All Sleep Disorder and All Disorder Combined groups
SOL All Sleep Disorder
For SOL diary there were k = 2 and N = 113, the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo SMD = -0.26, 95% CI [-0.61, 0.1], z = -1.4, p = 0.16. Therefore, this result indicates that that there is no difference in the effects of melatonin compared to placebo for SOL Diary scores in adults across sleep disorders.

Figure AB1: A forest plot to show the sensitivity analysis of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo for adults with sleep disorders

TST All Sleep Disorder
For TST diary there were k = 3 and N = 126 and the results indicated no significant difference between melatonin and placebo SMD = -0.25, 95% CI [-0.69, 0.2], z = -1.09, p = 0.28. Overall, this result indicates that that there is no difference in the effects of melatonin compared to placebo for TST Diary scores in adults across sleep disorders.

Figure AB2: A forest plot to show the sensitivity analysis of TST diary scores for melatonin against placebo for adults with sleep disorders


SOL All Disorder Combined
For SOL diary there were k = 3 and N = 153, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo SMD = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.69, -0.06], z = -2.36, p = 0.02. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 2) = 2.35, p = 0.31, τ = 0.002, I2 = 0.01% which means that this analysis produces an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, SOL diary scores appear to reduce after a treatment of melatonin compared to placebo in adults across all disorder. 



Figure AB3: A forest plot to show the sensitivity analysis of SOL diary scores for melatonin against placebo for adults across all disorders

TST All Disorder Combined

SOL
For SOL actigraphy there were k = 3 and N = 173, the results indicated a significant in favour of melatonin against placebo MD = -23.54, 95% CI [-35.23, -11.86], z = -3.95, p <.001. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 2) = 2.73, p =0.26, τ = 5.29, I2 = 30.95% which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes.  For SOL actigraphy there were k = 4 and N = 184, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = -9.72, 95% CI [-18.72, -0.63], z = -2.1, p = 0.04. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 3) = 7.13, p =0.07, τ = 7.12, I2 = 59.78% which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Overall, both SOL scores appear to reduce after a treatment of melatonin in comparison to placebo for all ages with DSPD.

For TST actigraphy there were k = 4 and N = 184, the results indicated a significant difference in favour of melatonin over placebo MD = 13.78, 95% CI [0.18, 27.39], z = 1.99, p = 0.05. Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity showed Q(df = 3) = 0.59, p =0.9, τ = 0, I2 = 0% which meant that this analysis produced an output which can account for variability of effect sizes. Therefore, these analyses indicate that both TST scores increase after a period of melatonin treatment in patients with DSPD, across all ages.
